# Summary: Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a Polish engineer and computer pioneer, born into a family of accomplished mountaineers and intellectuals. His early life was marked by adversity, including participation in the Polish resistance during World War II, multiple injuries, and recognition for bravery. After the war, he pursued studies in electrical engineering, eventually distinguishing himself through innovative designs in computing and electronics.
Karpiński's most significant contributions include the construction of the AAH harmonic analyzer (1957), the AKAT-1 differential equations analyzer (1959)—the first transistor-based device of its kind, and the development of Poland's perceptron (1964). He is especially notable for designing the high-speed KAR-65 computer (1968) and the groundbreaking K-202 minicomputer (1973). Despite K-202's technical superiority, political opposition, censorship, and lack of industrial support led to its limited production and commercial failure. Karpiński's career was marred by controversies, including accusations of espionage and later revelations of his work as a secret informant for Polish intelligence, which complicated his legacy. After spending time abroad and undertaking unsuccessful business ventures, he was recognized late in life with national honors for his work in computer engineering. His innovative machines are now preserved in museums, and his life has been chronicled in Polish literature and media.
